# How to use OpenCode with local models?

To use OpenCode with local models, you run a local inference server that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, then point OpenCode at that endpoint via a provider configuration and select the model in the UI. The key idea is that OpenCode doesn’t need the model to be “built in”; it needs a provider entry with a `baseURL` and a model name mapping so it can send chat/tool requests to the right place. OpenCode’s provider docs include explicit local examples (for example, Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp via a local server) that all follow the same shape: define a provider using an OpenAI-compatible SDK adapter and set `options.baseURL` to a localhost URL ending in `/v1`.

A practical workflow is: start your local model server first, confirm it’s listening, then configure OpenCode. For instance, with a local provider you’ll define something like `provider.ollama` (or `provider.lmstudio`) in your OpenCode config, set `npm` to an OpenAI-compatible adapter, set `options.baseURL` to the local endpoint (examples in the docs include `http://localhost:11434/v1` and `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1`), and list one or more models under `models` so they appear in OpenCode’s model picker. Then run `opencode`, use `/models` to pick your local model, and start working. If you want to keep things safe while you test, review your tool permissions: OpenCode tools can read/write files and run shell commands, and permissions control whether actions run automatically, are blocked, or require explicit approval. That matters more with local models because you might iterate quickly and forget you allowed a high-impact tool like shell execution.

Once local models are wired up, the “gotchas” are mostly operational: latency and capability depend on the model and your hardware, and you need your local endpoint to stay stable (port, hostname, firewall rules). If your model server runs on another machine (a home GPU box, for example), treat it like any internal service: use an SSH tunnel or a private network, and set `baseURL` to something reachable from your dev laptop without exposing it publicly. From a build-system perspective, local models pair nicely with local-first stacks: if you’re prototyping semantic search or long-term “project memory,” you can store embeddings in a local [Milvus](https://milvus.io/) instance during development and have OpenCode help you generate the ingestion/query code, then later switch to [Zilliz Cloud](https://zilliz.com/cloud) when you want managed hosting. The important part is not to confuse “OpenCode runs locally” with “everything runs locally by default”: you choose the boundary by choosing your model endpoint and your permissions, and OpenCode will follow that boundary.

web.title: Opencode for Agentic Development with Local LLMs
web.markdown:
Agentic development is rapidly transforming the way developers design, build, and ship software. Tools like Opencode let developers pair powerful local LLMs with intelligent agents to automate coding tasks, refactor large codebases, and accelerate development—all while keeping data private and within your own machine.

If you want to get started with Opencode using local LLMs (like Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma), here’s a simple, practical guide. before that, let's know

## Why OpenCode?

- **Agentic workflows** – AI agents that can modify your codebase intelligently.
- **Local-first development** – Integrate your own LLM running on GPU or CPU.
- **Extensibility** – Bring your own models, tools, and workflows.
- **Security & Privacy** – No proprietary code leaves your machine.

## Pre-requisites:

- Ollama
- GhostTTY
- Opencode

### Install and Run a Local LLM

- Go to [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) and follow the steps to install on your OS
- Add the desired LLM that supports agentic flow e.g. qwen3:8B, llama3.1:8b and so on. Check on ollama site.
- Run the following to install Qwen LLM to your local environment


```
ollama pull qwen3:8b
ollama list
ollama run qwen3:8b
```

Enter fullscreen modeExit fullscreen mode

- Now add the following tweaking to increase context window for agents to work properly.


```
ollama run <model_name>
>>> /set parameter num_ctx 32768
>>> /save <model_name>
```

Enter fullscreen modeExit fullscreen mode

### Install Ghostty

### Install OpenCode

Follow instructions on [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/) to install.

Once the pre-requisite steps are done. Now comes the execution part. First we need to add the LLM to the OpenCode config `opencode.json` file located at `.config/opencode/opencode.json` to work on.

```
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Execution

Now let's build something. Follow the steps:

- Open the ghostty terminal
- Create a directory for the application
- Run `opencode` inside the directory

I just build a tic-tac-toe game using the local LLM, although my CPUs are burning now 🔥 [Play here](https://ferdousulhaque.github.io/tic-tac-toe/)

## Benefits of Using Local LLMs

- Zero data leakage across the internet
- Better cost efficiency—no API billing
- Unlimited customization of models
- Offline development

web.markdown:
[![GPUhub logo](https://getdeploying.com/static/img/logos/gpuhub.c9dfcbd77dd6.png)GPUhubDedicated Bare-Metal GPUs. No Virtualization. No Shared Resources. Built for Stable AI Workloads.\\

Learn more →](https://gpuhub.com/?utm_source=getdeploying.com&utm_medium=paid&utm_content=banner-top)

OpenCode is an open-source, terminal-based coding agent similar to Claude Code or Cursor, but with support for local models. By pairing it with [LM Studio](https://getdeploying.com/guides/local-llm-mac-lm-studio), you can run a fully private coding assistant on your own hardware with no API keys or cloud dependencies.

This guide walks you through setting up LM Studio's local API server and connecting it to OpenCode.

Table of Contents

- [What you'll need](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#what-youll-need)
- [Starting the LM Studio API server](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#starting-the-lm-studio-api-server)
- [Installing OpenCode](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#installing-opencode)
- [Configuring OpenCode to use LM Studio](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#configuring-opencode-to-use-lm-studio)
- [Using OpenCode](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#using-opencode)
- [Switching between local and cloud models](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#switching-between-local-and-cloud-models)
- [Next steps](https://getdeploying.com/guides/lm-studio-opencode#next-steps)

## What you'll need

- **LM Studio** installed and running with a downloaded model. If you haven't set this up yet, follow the [LM Studio guide](https://getdeploying.com/guides/local-llm-mac-lm-studio) first.
- **Node.js** 18 or later (for installing OpenCode via npm), or use Homebrew.
- A model with strong instruction-following and code generation abilities. Recommended:

| RAM | Model | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 16GB | [qwen3.5-9b](https://lmstudio.ai/models/qwen/qwen3.5-9b) | Good all-rounder for code tasks |
| 24GB | [devstral-2](https://lmstudio.ai/models/devstral-2) | Mistral's dedicated coding agent model, strong at tool use and multi-step edits |
| 24GB+ | [qwen3-coder-next](https://lmstudio.ai/models/qwen3-coder-next) | Qwen's dedicated coding model, optimized for code generation and editing |
| 32GB+ | [qwen3.5-27b](https://lmstudio.ai/models/qwen/qwen3.5-27b) | Excellent code generation and reasoning at 27B parameters |
| 32GB+ | [gemma-4-31b](https://lmstudio.ai/models/google/gemma-4-31b) | Strong general-purpose model with large context window |

## Starting the LM Studio API server

LM Studio includes a built-in API server that is compatible with the OpenAI API format. OpenCode uses this to communicate with your local model.

1. Open LM Studio.
2. Load the model you want to use (click the Chat icon, then select a model from the dropdown).
3. Click the **Developer** tab on the left sidebar.
4. Toggle the server **On**. By default, it listens on `http://localhost:1234`.
5. Note the model identifier shown in the server panel (e.g., `qwen3.5-9b`). You'll need this for the OpenCode configuration.

You can verify the server is running:

```bash
curl http://localhost:1234/v1/models
```

Copy

You should see a JSON response listing the loaded model.

## Installing OpenCode

OpenCode can be installed via npm or Homebrew:

**npm:**

```bash
npm install -g opencode
```

Copy

**Homebrew:**

```bash
brew install opencode
```

Copy

Verify the installation:

```bash
opencode --version
```

Copy

## Configuring OpenCode to use LM Studio

OpenCode needs to know where your local API server is and which model to use. Create or edit the `opencode.json` configuration file in your project root:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "lmstudio": {
      "api": "openai",
      "baseURL": "http://localhost:1234/v1",
      "models": {
        "qwen3.5-9b": {
          "max_tokens": 8192,
          "context_length": 32768
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "model": {
    "provider": "lmstudio",
    "model": "qwen3.5-9b"
  }
}
```

Copy

Replace `qwen3.5-9b` with the model identifier shown in your LM Studio server panel if you're using a different model.

### Configuration notes

- **baseURL**: Points to LM Studio's local server. Change the port if you've configured a different one.
- **max\_tokens**: Maximum number of tokens per response. Increase this for longer code generation, but keep it within your model's limits.
- **context\_length**: The context window size. Check your model's specs in LM Studio. Larger values let OpenCode send more file content but use more memory.

## Using OpenCode

Navigate to your project directory and start OpenCode:

```bash
cd /path/to/your/project
opencode
```

Copy

OpenCode will launch an interactive terminal session. You can ask it to read, write, and modify files in your project, much like other AI coding assistants.

### Tips for local models

Local models have less capacity than large cloud models, so a few adjustments help:

- **Be specific.** Instead of "fix the bug," point to the file and describe the issue.
- **Work in small steps.** Ask for one change at a time rather than large refactors across multiple files.
- **Use capable models.** For complex code tasks, the 26B+ parameter models perform significantly better than smaller ones.
- **Keep context focused.** Smaller context windows mean OpenCode may struggle with very large files. Break big files into smaller modules when possible.

## Switching between local and cloud models

One of OpenCode's strengths is supporting multiple providers. You can configure both a local model and a cloud provider in the same `opencode.json` and switch between them:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "lmstudio": {
      "api": "openai",
      "baseURL": "http://localhost:1234/v1",
      "models": {
        "qwen3.5-9b": {
          "max_tokens": 8192,
          "context_length": 32768
        }
      }
    },
    "anthropic": {
      "models": {
        "claude-sonnet-4-6": {
          "max_tokens": 16384,
          "context_length": 200000
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "model": {
    "provider": "lmstudio",
    "model": "qwen3.5-9b"
  }
}
```

Copy

Switch to the cloud model by changing the `model` section, or use the model picker inside OpenCode's UI. This gives you a practical workflow: iterate locally for free during development, then switch to a more powerful cloud model when you need it.

## Next steps

- **Try different models.** Swap between smaller and larger models in LM Studio to find the best speed-vs-quality tradeoff for your workflow.
- **Use the local API in other tools.** LM Studio's OpenAI-compatible server works with any tool that supports custom OpenAI endpoints, not just OpenCode.
- **Explore OpenCode's features.** Check the [OpenCode documentation](https://opencode.ai/) for features like file watching, custom system prompts, and tool use.
- **Compare cloud GPU options.** When you need more power than your local hardware can provide, check out [cloud GPU prices](https://getdeploying.com/gpus) and [LLM API prices](https://getdeploying.com/llms) to find the best option.

No API keys copied into config files. No fighting stale setup.** [Get started](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#get-started) · [See how it works](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#what-happens-behind-the-scenes) · [Troubleshooting](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/docs/troubleshooting.md) * * * ## What problem does this solve? [Permalink: What problem does this solve?](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#what-problem-does-this-solve) OpenCode works beautifully with built-in providers. Local models are a little messier. You load a different model in LM Studio. You restart Ollama. You move vLLM to another machine. The model name changes, but your OpenCode configuration does not. **OpenCode Local Setup keeps the two in sync.** When you open OpenCode, it checks the model servers you configured, discovers what is actually available, and updates only the relevant part of your `opencode.json`. ``` Your model server → discovers live models → OpenCode is ready ``` It leaves the rest of your OpenCode setup alone. ## Get started [Permalink: Get started](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#get-started) ### 1\. Install OpenCode [Permalink: 1. Install OpenCode](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#1-install-opencode) ``` curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash ``` ### 2\. Install this helper [Permalink: 2. Install this helper](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#2-install-this-helper) ``` git clone https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup.git cd opencode-local-setup ./scripts/install.sh ``` ### 3\. Start your model server and open OpenCode [Permalink: 3. Start your model server and open OpenCode](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#3-start-your-model-server-and-open-opencode) ``` opencode ``` That is it. The default setup looks for LM Studio at: ``` http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1 ``` Inside OpenCode, use `/models` to choose a model. Note This project connects OpenCode to your model server. It does not install LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, or the models themselves. ## Pick the setup you use [Permalink: Pick the setup you use](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#pick-the-setup-you-use) | You run | Start with | Helper command | | --- | --- | --- | | **LM Studio** | `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1` | `oc-lmstudio` | | **Ollama** | `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` | `oc-ollama` | | **vLLM** | `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1` | `oc-vllm` | | **llama.cpp** | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1` | `oc-llamacpp` | | **Remote GPU server** | Any reachable OpenAI-compatible URL | Add it to `opencode.json` | The helper commands synchronize that server and launch OpenCode: ``` oc-ollama oc-vllm oc-lmstudio "Review this repository" ``` They are prefixed with `oc-`, so they never replace the real `ollama`, `vllm`, or server commands on your computer. ## What you get [Permalink: What you get](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#what-you-get) ### Your model list stays fresh [Permalink: Your model list stays fresh](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#your-model-list-stays-fresh) Load or remove a model on the server and OpenCode sees the change on the next sync. ### Your existing configuration is respected [Permalink: Your existing configuration is respected](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#your-existing-configuration-is-respected) The synchronizer updates provider models without replacing unrelated settings, agents, MCP servers, permissions, themes, or keybindings. ### Secrets stay out of the file [Permalink: Secrets stay out of the file](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#secrets-stay-out-of-the-file) API keys remain in environment variables or OpenCode's own credential store. Generated provider entries use safe references such as: ``` "apiKey": "{env:REMOTE_API_KEY}" ``` ### Local and remote machines work the same way [Permalink: Local and remote machines work the same way](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#local-and-remote-machines-work-the-same-way) A model can run on your laptop, desktop, home server, LAN workstation, or trusted Tailscale machine. If the endpoint is reachable and OpenAI-compatible, it can be synchronized. ### It is designed to fail quietly [Permalink: It is designed to fail quietly](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#it-is-designed-to-fail-quietly) A sleeping GPU box or closed LM Studio window should not stop OpenCode from opening. Launch checks use short timeouts and skip unavailable endpoints. ## What happens behind the scenes? [Permalink: What happens behind the scenes?](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#what-happens-behind-the-scenes) Render lists available models updates only provider models safe secret references Your model server OpenCode Local Setup Your opencode.json OpenCode Environment variables Loading ``` flowchart LR A[Your model server] -->|lists available models| B[OpenCode Local Setup] B -->|updates only provider models| C[Your opencode.json] C --> D[OpenCode] E[Environment variables] -->|safe secret references| C ``` In plain English: 1. It reads the OpenCode configuration you already use. 2. It accepts normal JSON or JSONC with comments and trailing commas. 3. It asks each configured server for its live model list. 4. It refreshes model names and supported metadata. 5. It removes models that are no longer served, unless configured otherwise. 6. It writes the file safely and keeps it private to your user account. ## Commands you will actually use [Permalink: Commands you will actually use](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#commands-you-will-actually-use) ``` opencode # Open OpenCode with a quick pre-launch sync sync-models # Refresh your configured compatible servers opencode models # Show available provider/model IDs opencode models --refresh # Refresh OpenCode's built-in provider cache opencode auth login # Connect a built-in cloud provider oc-doctor # Check config health and secret hygiene opencode upgrade # Upgrade OpenCode ``` ## Change the default server [Permalink: Change the default server](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#change-the-default-server) Edit the small environment file created by the installer: ``` $EDITOR ~/.config/opencode/local-setup/.env.local ``` For example: ``` LOCAL_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 OPENCODE_PROVIDER_ID=ollama OPENCODE_PROVIDER_NAME="Ollama" ``` Then run: ``` sync-models ``` ## Connect a remote GPU machine [Permalink: Connect a remote GPU machine](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#connect-a-remote-gpu-machine) Add a provider to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`: ``` { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "provider": { "gpu-box": { "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible", "name": "My GPU Box", "options": { "baseURL": "http://100.100.100.100:8000/v1", "apiKey": "{env:REMOTE_API_KEY}" }, "models": {} } } } ``` Export the key only when the server requires one: ``` export REMOTE_API_KEY="your-key" sync-models ``` Tailscale discovery is available for trusted networks, but remains off by default. Explicit providers work without any scanning. **Enable narrowly scoped Tailscale discovery** ``` export OPENCODE_TAILSCALE_DISCOVERY=1 export OPENCODE_TAILSCALE_PORTS=1234,8000,8080,11434 sync-models ``` Only online peers and the ports you list are checked. ## Safe by default [Permalink: Safe by default](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#safe-by-default) - Raw API keys are not written into generated configuration. - Existing OpenCode settings are preserved. - Config updates are atomic, reducing the chance of a half-written file. - File permissions are restricted to your user. - Tailscale discovery is opt-in. - Post-exit synchronization is opt-in. - Automatic session sharing is not enabled. Run the built-in health check whenever something feels wrong: ``` oc-doctor ``` ## Already installed an older version? [Permalink: Already installed an older version?](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#already-installed-an-older-version) ``` cd opencode-local-setup git pull ./scripts/install.sh oc-doctor ``` Your existing `opencode.json` and local environment file are preserved. ## Built for people who [Permalink: Built for people who](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#built-for-people-who) - Run private or local models while coding. - Swap models frequently in LM Studio or Ollama. - Serve models with vLLM or llama.cpp. - Use a separate GPU workstation or home server. - Want a clean OpenCode setup without maintaining model IDs by hand. ## For contributors [Permalink: For contributors](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#for-contributors) ``` npm run validate ``` The validation suite covers JSONC parsing, model metadata migration, secure credential handling, atomic writes, multi-provider refresh, installation behavior, and opt-in Tailscale discovery. ## More documentation [Permalink: More documentation](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#more-documentation) - [Configuration and script reference](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/docs/api-reference.md) - [Authentication and credentials](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/docs/auth-providers.md) - [Troubleshooting](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/docs/troubleshooting.md) - [Example configurations](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/configs) ## License [Permalink: License](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#license) [MIT](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup/blob/master/LICENSE) ## About OpenCode local AI provider setup with automatic model syncing for LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible API ### Resources [Readme](https://github.com/groxaxo/opencode-local-setup#readme-ov-file) ### Uh oh! [![zephel01](https://assets.st-note.com/production/uploads/images/176573832/profile_7cc56f5f747f0682878cf9d359da99e8.jpg?width=60)](https://note.com/zephel01)

## Introduction

Once you start using OpenCode, you will begin to worry about the following two things:

- **Cloud API costs (usage-based billing/limits/contracts)**

- **External transmission of code and design information (privacy/company policy)**


This is where **“OpenCode × Local LLM”** comes in handy. By keeping your daily work local and only offloading to the cloud when absolutely necessary, you can achieve:

- ✅ Run most of your daily coding **for just the cost of electricity**

- ✅ **Ensure privacy** by not sending code externally

- ✅ Switch to **powerful cloud models only when needed** for design/difficult bugs/final reviews


all at the same time.

* * *

## Mechanism: OpenCode switches via "provider" rather than "environment variables"

Instead of replacing ANTHROPIC\_BASE\_URL like in Claude Code, the standard way to switch in OpenCode is to **define the provider (connection destination) and model in opencode.json**. ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Furthermore, API keys are registered via **/connect** and saved locally (when using the cloud). ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

* * *

## STEP 1 — Prepare a local server (LM Studio / Ollama / vLLM)

The shortest route to connect from OpenCode to local is to use **OpenAI-compatible API (/v1)**. Including LiteLLM, current peripheral tools tend to converge here. ( [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/openai_compatible?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### Method A: LM Studio (with GUI, easiest)

Start LM Studio in Server mode and ensure it is outputting an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for example:

- http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1


Verification:

```
curl http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models
```

copy

### Method B: Ollama (CLI, lightweight)

There is an increasing number of configurations where Ollama can also be treated as OpenAI-compatible (though activation/configuration may be required depending on the environment). First, aim for the goal of being able to "hit the OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint" to avoid confusion.

* * *

## STEP 2 — Create the OpenCode configuration (opencode.json)

OpenCode can be configured via opencode.json / opencode.jsonc. ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Here, we will define "Local (LM Studio)" and "Cloud (Anthropic)" and **fix the model switching to a form that is easy to manage**.

> **Point**: The provider's baseURL can be specified in options.baseURL. ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
>
> However, inconsistencies such as "Other (Custom)" not appearing in /connect have been reported (behavior may change depending on the OpenCode version). ( [GitHub](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/5937?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### For copy-paste: ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc

```
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",

  "provider": {
    "lmstudio": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "LM Studio (local)",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        // ★ここはあなたの環境で見える model id に合わせて書く
        // curl http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models で確認
        "qwen3-coder-30b": { "name": "Qwen3 Coder 30B (local)" },
        "glm-4.7-flash": { "name": "GLM-4.7-Flash (local)" },
        "devstral-small-2": { "name": "Devstral Small 2 (local)" }
      }
    },

    "anthropic": {
      "name": "Anthropic",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://api.anthropic.com/v1"
      }
    }
  },

  // デフォルト（普段はローカル）
  "model": "lmstudio/qwen3-coder-30b",
  "small_model": "lmstudio/glm-4.7-flash",

  // 役割別に固定（迷わない運用のため）
  "agent": {
    "local-heavy": {
      "description": "ローカル高品質（普段の実装）",
      "model": "lmstudio/qwen3-coder-30b",
      "mode": "primary"
    },
    "local-light": {
      "description": "ローカル軽量（雑タスク）",
      "model": "lmstudio/glm-4.7-flash",
      "mode": "primary"
    },
    "opus": {
      "description": "クラウド最強（設計/難バグ/最終レビュー）",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-5-20251101",
      "mode": "primary"
    },
    "sonnet": {
      "description": "クラウド高速（広めの作業）",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
      "mode": "primary"
    }
  }
}
```

copy

* * *

## STEP 3 — Register keys via /connect when using the cloud

When using cloud services like Anthropic, enter authentication via OpenCode's /connect (saved locally). ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

* * *

## STEP 4 — How to use (switching workflow)

### Launch OpenCode

```
opencode
```

copy

### Launch by specifying a model (provider/model)

```
opencode -m lmstudio/qwen3-coder-30b
```

copy

### Standardize "Local for daily use, Cloud for critical tasks" (Recommended)

- Daily: local-heavy (Local 30B class)

- Casual tasks: local-light (Local lightweight)

- Design/Difficult bugs/Final review: opus / sonnet


* * *

## For advanced users: Automate routing with LiteLLM (Works great with OpenCode)

If you want to flexibly manage multiple backends, it is powerful to use **LiteLLM Proxy** as a "unified gateway".

- OpenCode → LiteLLM (OpenAI-compatible) → Various local/cloud models

- This allows you to consolidate **adding/removing connection targets** and **key management** on the LiteLLM side

- LiteLLM operates as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint ( [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/user_keys?utm_source=chatgpt.com))


## STEP A — Create the LiteLLM configuration file

~/litellm-config.yaml Example (Slightly formatted your original text for OpenCode):

```
# ~/litellm-config.yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: local
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/qwen3-coder-30b
      api_base: http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1
      api_key: lmstudio

  - model_name: opus
    litellm_params:
      model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-5-20251101
      api_key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}

  - model_name: lite
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-oss-20b
      api_base: http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1
      api_key: lmstudio
```

copy

- The philosophy of “consolidating OpenAI-compatible upstreams” is central to the official LiteLLM documentation. ( [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/configs?utm_source=chatgpt.com))


## STEP B — Start the Proxy

```
pip install "litellm[proxy]"
litellm --config ~/litellm-config.yaml --port 4000
```

copy

## STEP C — Connect to LiteLLM from OpenCode (opencode.json)

On the OpenCode side, register LiteLLM as an **“OpenAI-compatible provider”** (point the baseURL to 4000). ( [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/providers/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

```
{
  "provider": {
    "litellm": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "LiteLLM Gateway",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "local": { "name": "Local (via LiteLLM)" },
        "opus": { "name": "Opus (via LiteLLM)" },
        "lite": { "name": "Lite local (via LiteLLM)" }
      }
    }
  },

  "model": "litellm/local",
  "small_model": "litellm/lite"
}
```

copy

With this, from OpenCode,

- litellm/local (local high-performance)

- litellm/opus (Opus)

- litellm/lite (local lightweight)


can all be unified using the “same connection method.”

* * *

## Troubleshooting (OpenCode Version)

### Cannot connect (Check local/LM Studio side)

```
curl http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models
```

copy

### Suspicious behavior via LiteLLM (Check LiteLLM side)

```
curl http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models
```

copy

### Model response is slow

- In LM Studio settings, set **GPU Offload to maximum** (within the limits of your VRAM)

- Lower the quantization to **Q4 series (e.g., Q4\_K\_M)** to balance speed and quality

- Keep the context length to the absolute minimum (increasing it tends to slow things down)


### The provider “Other (Custom)” does not appear in /connect

- This has been reported. Since there are improvements/fluctuations with OpenCode updates, it is best to check the relevant Issue or the behavior of the latest version. ( [GitHub](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/5937?utm_source=chatgpt.com))


* * *

## Cost reduction estimate (guideline)

[![画像](https://assets.st-note.com/img/1770834540-02vzRKVCFyaDOSgUXrq5wZk6.png?width=1200)](https://assets.st-note.com/img/1770834540-02vzRKVCFyaDOSgUXrq5wZk6.png?width=2000&height=2000&fit=bounds&quality=85)

Conclusion: **80% local, 20% cloud** is the best way to balance “time and quality.”

* * *

## Recommended Local Models (Latest for Late 2025–2026)

The evolution of local coding models is extremely fast, and from the second half of 2025 through the end of the year, powerful new models have appeared one after another. **All are MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) or compact dense matrix models,** running on fewer resources than their apparent parameter counts suggest.

### 🏆 High-Performance Models Running on Consumer GPUs (Recommended Range)

**Qwen3-Coder 30B (Q4\_K\_M)**

- **Architecture:** MoE / 30B total parameters, 3.3B active during inference

- **Context:** 256K tokens (native)

- **VRAM:** Approx. 15–19GB with Q4 quantization

- **Features:** Top-class among open models on SWE-bench Verified, Japanese language support, 256K ultra-long context, and training specialized for agents (long-term RL)

- **Claude Code Integration:** Official support for Ollama, starts immediately with ollama run qwen3-coder:30b

- **Summary:** The “default candidate” for daily coding tasks. Since it is an MoE, it runs even with low VRAM.


```
ollama run qwen3-coder:30b
```

copy

**Qwen3-Coder-Next (80B-A3B)** ⭐ New Arrival (Late 2025)

- **Architecture:** Hybrid attention + high-sparsity MoE / 80B total, 3B active

- **Context:** 256K tokens

- **VRAM:** Because active parameters are 3B, it can run on under 24GB with MoE offloading

- **Features:** Trained with large-scale agent RL based on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Base. **The official claim is that despite having only 3B active parameters, it performs on par with models 10–20 times its size.** Explicitly supports IDE integration with Claude Code / Qwen Code / Cline, etc.

- **Summary:** A superior version of the 30B model. If you have sufficient hardware, choose this without hesitation.


```
# vLLM / SGLang 推奨（Ollama 対応は随時確認）
python -m sglang.launch_server --model Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next \
  --tp-size 2 --port 30000 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
```

copy

**GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B)** ⭐ Released December 2025

- **Developer:** Z.AI (Zhipu AI)

- **Architecture:** MoE / 30B Total, 3B Active

- **Context:** 128K tokens

- **VRAM:** **approx. 15GB** with Q4 quantization

- **Benchmarks:** SWE-bench 59.2% (highest among open 30B-class models), τ²-bench 79.5% (tool-calling performance equivalent to Claude 3.5 Sonnet), AIME 2025 91.6%

- **Features:** A practical model positioned by Z.AI as an "open model equivalent to Haiku." Trained specifically for coding and tool usage. Supports switching to thinking mode.

- **Notes:** Requires the --tool-call-parser glm47 flag when launching with vLLM / SGLang


```
# vLLM での起動
vllm serve zai-org/GLM-4.7-Flash \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 \
  --reasoning-parser glm45 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --served-model-name glm-4.7-flash \
  --port 8000
```

copy

```
# Claude Code から接続
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000
claude --model glm-4.7-flash
```

copy

**Devstral Small 2 (24B)** ⭐ Released December 2025

- **Developer:** Mistral AI

- **Architecture:** Dense transformer

- **Context:** 256K tokens

- **VRAM:** Approx. **25GB** at Q8 full precision, 12–14GB for Q4

- **Benchmark:** SWE-bench Verified **68.0%** (Remarkable for a 24B model. Equivalent to models 5x larger)

- **License:** Apache 2.0 (Commercial use OK)

- **Features:** Vision support (can analyze code screenshots), specialized for multi-file operations and codebase exploration. A smaller version of Devstral 2 (123B full model) and a top candidate for **the strongest coding model that runs on consumer hardware**


```

ollama run devstral-small-2
```

- **Features:** SWE-bench 68.0%, vision support, 256K context

- **Use Case:** Multi-file operations, codebase exploration


**Balanced: Qwen2.5-Coder 32B**

- **Memory Usage:** Approx. 18GB

- **Speed:** Slightly slow (12-18 tokens/s)

- **Features:** Coding-specialized, highest quality

- **Use Case:** Production code generation, scenarios requiring high quality


```

ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b            # メイン（高品質）
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b          # サブ（中間タスク用）
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b           # 軽量（簡単なタスク用）
```

### 💡 Practical Advice by Memory Size

Tips for 16GB Environments

**Efficiency through using multiple models for different tasks**

```
# 簡単なタスク → Phi-3 Mini（超高速）
alias cc-lite='claude --model phi3:mini'

# 通常タスク → Qwen2.5-Coder 7B
alias cc='claude --model qwen2.5-coder:7b'
```

copy

**Memory-saving techniques:**

- Set context length to the minimum necessary (reduce from default 16K to 8K)

- Close unused applications

- Reduce browser tabs


Optimization for 32GB Environments

**Automatic switching based on tasks**

```
# 日常作業
alias cc='claude --model qwen2.5-coder:14b'

# 難しいデバッグ
alias cc-debug='claude --model deepseek-r1-distill-qwen:14b'

# 軽量タスク

```

How to Utilize 64GB Environments

**Simultaneous use of multiple models**

```
# メインターミナル: 高品質モデル
claude --model qwen3-coder:30b

# サブターミナル: 軽量モデル（検証用）

```

**Strategy for combined use with the cloud**

- 90% of daily tasks → Local (Qwen3-Coder 30B)

- 10% of complex design → Opus (Cloud)

- Cost reduction rate: approx. 85%


## Summary

The setup for using local LLMs with Claude Code is surprisingly simple, requiring only a change to environment variables.

### Key takeaways from this article

1. Connect to local by simply rewriting ANTHROPIC\_BASE\_URL

2. Make it easy to switch models using profiles in ~/.claude/settings.json

3. Switch with one command like cc-opus using shell aliases

4. Use local for daily tasks and cloud for difficult designs


### The settings I actually use

```
# 普段はこれ（ローカル）
alias cc='claude'

# ここぞという時だけ
alias cc-opus='claude --profile opus'
```

opencode-local-provider OpenCode Plugin](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#opencode-local-provider-opencode-plugin) OpenCode plugin that adds a single `local` provider with runtime model detection for local OpenAI-compatible servers. It currently supports the following local backends: - Ollama - LM Studio - llama.cpp server - vLLM - Exo - llama-swap - oMLX - MLX-VLM Instead of creating one provider per server, this plugin keeps one `local` provider and lets you register multiple named targets. Each target is probed at runtime, and its currently loaded models are exposed automatically. ## Features [Permalink: Features](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#features) - Adds a `local` provider to OpenCode - Supports multiple local URLs under one provider - Includes supported default `127.0.0.1` targets automatically - Detects loaded models at runtime - Routes each model to the correct target URL - API key auth currently unsupported - Uses OpenCode global config, not project-local config ## Example [Permalink: Example](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#example) screenrecording-2026-04-07\_01-16-56.mp4 ## Install [Permalink: Install](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#install) ``` opencode plugin --global opencode-local-provider ``` OpenCode will install the package and update the config for you. ## Provider Setup [Permalink: Provider Setup](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#provider-setup) Default targets are enabled automatically for these backends and ports: - Ollama: `http://127.0.0.1:11434` - LM Studio: `http://127.0.0.1:1234` - llama.cpp: `http://127.0.0.1:8080` - vLLM: `http://127.0.0.1:8000` - Exo: `http://127.0.0.1:52415` - llama-swap: `http://127.0.0.1:8080` - oMLX: `http://127.0.0.1:8000` - MLX-VLM: `http://127.0.0.1:8000` If your local providers do not need auth, you can start using the `local` provider immediately. **Note: oMLX requires API authentication to be disabled in the web app settings for the plugin to detect and probe models.** **Note: API key authentication is currently unsupported.** ## Custom Targets [Permalink: Custom Targets](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#custom-targets) If you need non-default hosts or ports, use the CLI auth flow to add an explicit target: ``` opencode auth login --provider local --method "Add Custom Target" ``` This will prompt for: - a target ID, like `studio` or `remote-ollama` - the local provider URL - the API key (enter `none` since API keys are currently unsupported) The target is then stored in OpenCode global config. You can also add explicit targets manually in config if needed: ``` { "provider": { "local": { "name": "Local Provider", "options": { "includeDefaults": true, "targets": { "studio": { "url": "http://192.168.1.10:1234/v1", "kind": "lmstudio" } } } } } } ``` Explicit targets override the built-in defaults when they use the same ID. The CLI custom-target method is the supported way to add explicit targets without editing config directly. ## Resulting Config [Permalink: Resulting Config](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#resulting-config) The plugin stores explicit targets in OpenCode global config under the `local` provider: ``` { "provider": { "local": { "name": "Local Provider", "options": { "includeDefaults": true, "targets": { "studio": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1", "kind": "lmstudio" } } } } } } ``` With `includeDefaults: true`, the built-in default `127.0.0.1` targets are also checked at runtime even though they are not written into config. **Note: API key authentication is currently unsupported.** ## How Models Appear [Permalink: How Models Appear](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#how-models-appear) Models are discovered dynamically from each configured target. (Only **loaded** models) To avoid collisions, model IDs are prefixed with the target ID: - `ollama/llama3.2` - `studio/qwen2.5-coder` Each generated model keeps its own target URL internally, so requests go to the correct backend. ## Notes [Permalink: Notes](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#notes) - Model detection is runtime-based, not static - If loaded models change in your local server, OpenCode will see the updated list on the next provider refresh - Built-in default `127.0.0.1` targets are enabled unless you set `includeDefaults` to `false` - **API key authentication is currently unsupported** ## Development [Permalink: Development](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#development) Build the plugin: ``` bun run build ``` Run the provider integration suite: ``` bun run test:providers ``` Run a single provider suite: ``` PROVIDER_SUITE=ollama bun run test:providers ``` Notes: - The suite starts provider containers for `ollama`, `lmstudio`, `llamacpp`, `vllm`, `exo`, `llamaswap`, `omlx`, and `mlxvlm` from `tests/docker/compose.providers.yml`. - The Bun test runner talks to each service over the Docker Compose network using each container's internal IP. It does not require publishing ports to the host. - The first run can be slow because the containers may need to download model assets, LM Studio bootstraps its headless runtime at startup, and Exo warms models to a real ready state before the suite proceeds. - CI runs the same suite per provider via `.github/workflows/provider-tests.yml`. - If you change provider models or startup behavior, update `tests/docker/compose.providers.yml` and the Bun orchestration helpers in `tests/docker/` instead of duplicating those details here. Install it locally in OpenCode with a file path plugin entry, for example: ``` opencode plugin $PWD ``` ## License [Permalink: License](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#license) MIT ## About OpenCode Plugin for Local LLM Servers ### Resources [Readme](https://github.com/goniz/opencode-local-provider#readme-ov-file) ### Uh oh!
